overview: The server is the authority for accounts, conversation visibility, messages and durable events. One workspace folder holds SQLite plus attachment blobs; an exclusive writer hold keeps schedulers and storage accounting consistent. The protocol package supplies shared data shapes, request validation and small policies so web, desktop and server agree. Recent work removes redundant private content, contains malformed logging, bounds callback lifetimes and protects delayed replies. The further review's Q01 restore publication race is closed by a path lock held through the folder swap.

entries.plain: Scrambles passwords so they are never saved as typed, and makes the secret keys that keep people signed in.
entries.summary: Derives password credentials and turns bearer tokens into database lookup keys.
details: Passwords use asynchronous scrypt with a fresh 16-byte random salt and a 64-byte derived key; verification compares equal-length buffers with timingSafeEqual.
A new session returns a random 32-byte token to the caller and its SHA-256 hash for storage. Knowing a stored session hash does not provide the original bearer token.
The module contains cryptographic primitives; expiry, deactivation, session revocation and request admission belong to Store and server.ts.

entries.plain: Makes a complete backup of the workspace and its files, checks it, and puts a backup back in place when the host restores one.
entries.summary: Captures, verifies, inventories and restores portable workspace backups.
details: VACUUM INTO captures a consistent SQLite snapshot including committed WAL content. Only blobs referenced by that snapshot are copied; a disappearing or wrong-sized referenced blob fails capture.

A staged capture is checked before publication. The manifest records schema, counts, SHA-256 checksums and attachment sizes; verification also checks integrity, foreign keys, duplicate names and containment.
inventoryBackup reads older schemas without upgrading them and explains external app destinations, waiting schedules, undelivered events and surviving sessions before a copy is started.
Restore verifies source and staged bytes, moves the old workspace to a superseded folder and publishes the replacement. It preserves the old copy for recovery instead of deleting it.

Q01: restore holds a path lock beside the target through staging, both renames and rollback. The in-folder hold is still released before the renames, since Windows cannot rename a folder with an open file in it, but a concurrent server start or second restore is refused without creating the target.

entries.plain: Turns the text, buttons and forms that Slack-style apps send into what Tandem can show, leaving out what it cannot.
entries.summary: Converts supported Slack Block Kit payloads into Tandem's text, buttons and modal fields.
details: Headers, sections, context and dividers flatten into the existing mrkdwn renderer. Explicit nonempty text wins over blocks, matching the expected fallback behavior.
Only buttons from actions blocks become MessageAction records; labels, values and count are bounded, styles normalized and link URLs restricted to HTTP(S).

Modal parsing keeps plain text, multiline text and static selects, caps fields/options and reports dropped fields. A view with no usable inputs is refused by the server rather than presented as a misleading empty form.
This is a deliberate subset adapter, not a complete Slack UI renderer; unsupported controls are omitted.

entries.plain: Briefly remembers which open forms and replies an app is still allowed to use, and forgets them when the server restarts.
entries.summary: Keeps short-lived app permissions in a bounded in-memory map.
details: Response URLs, triggers and open views carry expiresAt; get removes expired values before returning them.
Insertion sweeps expired entries from the oldest end, then evicts oldest entries above the ceiling. Equal lifetime within each map makes early-stop expiration sweeping valid.
Replacing a key moves it to the newest position. Eviction is treated like expiry, so memory cannot grow with every user and integration forever.
These capabilities intentionally disappear on server restart; they are separate from durable messages and event-delivery rows.

entries.plain: Gives every workspace the built-in /shrug and /me commands, even before any app is added.
entries.summary: Provides built-in /shrug and /me commands before any integration is installed.
details: A map holds description, usage hint and a function that returns the message text or null for invalid arguments.
/shrug escapes its backslash and underscores through the shared formatter so the visible arms survive mrkdwn parsing; /me wraps supplied text in italics.
Built-in names are reserved during app command registration, preventing an app from unexpectedly taking over these commands.

entries.plain: Checks the host's startup settings, such as the port and public address, and says clearly what to fix when one is wrong.
entries.summary: Rejects unusable startup settings with actionable messages.
details: Environment settings prefer TANDEM_, then GATHERLINE_, then SLACKOSS_ names, retaining compatibility with earlier deployments.
Port parsing requires a whole number from 0 to 65535; zero requests an available port. Count settings require safe nonnegative integers rather than silently rounded fractions.
Public URLs must use HTTP(S) without credentials, query or fragment because these addresses are handed to apps and shared as links.
Common bind failures are translated into suggestions such as choosing another port or a valid local interface.
keptSettingsNotes says, a line for each, which of --name, --access-policy and --invite-only an owned workspace did not take, and that owners and admins change them in Workspace settings.

entries.plain: Sets up the workspace's database and upgrades it to the newest layout, keeping a copy of the old one first.
entries.summary: Defines the SQLite schema history and safely opens or upgrades a workspace.
details: SQLite opens with WAL, foreign keys and a busy timeout. All needed migration steps run in one transaction, so failure rolls back to the original schema and releases the file handle.

An existing database receives a consistent pre-upgrade copy before migration by default. Up to three recognized restorable copies are retained; damaged or unrelated files do not displace a usable copy.
Schema 37 removes actions from deleted messages and superseded/purged replay copies, and blanks text/file IDs from sent schedules. Current live buttons and every unsent schedule remain usable.
Indexes support mention lookup, delegated managers and due cleanup/retry work instead of repeated broad scans.
A newer schema is refused by an older build. Logical cleanup affects active database records; it does not promise erasure of historical backups or freed disk bytes.
Schema 39 adds users.status_expires_at, when a status clears itself, or NULL for one kept until changed (UX-61).

Schema 40 adds channel_members.starred, one member's star on a conversation (UX-20). It sits on the membership beside muted, so leaving drops it, joining again starts unstarred, and an archived channel keeps it.

entries.plain: Notes the last 500 huddle joins, leaves and connection problems so owners and admins can look into a failed call.
entries.summary: Keeps the latest 500 lines of what happened in huddles, in memory, for the host.
details: Lines are joins, leaves, setups passed on or dropped, and each side's report of its connection; nothing survives a restart, and none is an address, an SDP or anything said in a call.
Read through GET /api/admin/calls by the owner and admins, filtered to conversations the reader can access.

entries.plain: Keeps each app's live connection open, catches it up after a reconnect, and sends each update only to people allowed to see it.
entries.summary: Authenticates sockets, reconstructs state on reconnect and delivers authorized live events.
details: An initial hello checks protocol version, token, account state and forced password change before the socket joins fan-out. The ready snapshot is read completely first.

A reconnect receives authorized missed events when its cursor remains replayable; otherwise the sync contract replaces history. syncVersion 1 ends with a synced marker so clients know catch-up finished.
Public channel events can reach all signed-in readers; private and DM events require current membership. Session authorization is rechecked after admission, including heartbeat and delivery paths.
byUser groups a person's sockets for targeted updates. Presence lists only online accounts, avoiding a second full offline-account listing at every handshake.
Huddles and typing are ephemeral. Signaling relays only between authorized participants in the same huddle; the server carries signaling, not media.

Socket callbacks contain thrown failures and close the affected connection with a retryable server error. Heartbeats, authentication timeout, payload limits and idempotent close bound abandoned connections.

Writes huddle joins, refusals, departures with their reason, relayed offers and answers, signals it could not pass on and why, and clients' huddle.report summaries to an in-memory CallLog; the ready snapshot advertises huddleReports.
The ready snapshot also advertises stars, so a client offers Star only where it is kept (UX-20).
The ready snapshot advertises workspaceSettings and says accessPolicy, so a client offers Workspace settings' controls only where the server takes them (UX-60).

entries.plain: Creates time-ordered IDs for messages and other records, plus random invite codes and secret keys for apps.
entries.summary: Creates sortable entity IDs and random invitation/integration secrets.
details: ULID-style IDs combine a Crockford-base32 timestamp with random characters, letting ordinary lexicographic comparisons support time-ordered history paging.

Messages take orderedUlid: within one millisecond it counts up from the previous random half instead of drawing a new one, so ids sort in the order the messages were made. History pages and client lists order by id, and two messages in one millisecond used to sort either way round. Its ids are easy to guess from a neighbour, so nothing that acts as a capability uses it.
Invitation codes use a short readable alphabet; bot and webhook secrets use longer random hex tokens with an optional prefix.
An ID is a reference, while a secret token grants a specific authority. The two must not be treated as interchangeable by callers.

entries.plain: Reads an uploaded picture's width and height so the conversation can save room for it and not jump while it loads.
entries.summary: Reads image dimensions from headers without loading a native decoder.
details: PNG, GIF, WebP variants and JPEG frame headers are recognized; unsupported shapes return null.
The resulting dimensions are attached to file metadata so the client can reserve image space before decoding and reduce timeline layout jumps.
It extracts dimensions, not a proof that the whole file is a valid or trustworthy image.

entries.plain: The front door to the server's code, which the desktop app uses to run a workspace or make backups.
entries.summary: Defines the server package's public API for desktop embedding and tooling.
details: Exports server creation/options, Store, workspace holds, backup/recovery-adjacent operations and shared security policies.
Consumers can embed a workspace server or perform offline backup operations without importing the CLI entry point and executing argument parsing.
Explicit type exports keep the package boundary readable and allow desktop adapters to depend on stable contracts.

entries.plain: Signs what the server sends to outside apps and rewrites workspace events in the form Slack apps expect.
entries.summary: Signs outbound callbacks and adapts durable native events to Slack's event shape.
details: HMAC-SHA256 signs v0:timestamp:body and emits both SlackOSS and Slack header names, allowing existing receiver verification libraries to work.
Message, reaction, pin, membership, channel and user events map to supported Slack Events API payloads; unsupported native events return null.
eventActorId identifies the account behind applicable events so the dispatcher can avoid feeding a bot its own actions and creating reply loops.
Receiver code still needs to enforce timestamp freshness and deduplication; signing alone does not eliminate replay or repeated delivery.

entries.plain: Slows down password guessing and floods of requests, while still letting an app back from offline send its waiting messages.
entries.summary: Rations abusive workloads while allowing normal startup and offline-outbox bursts.
details: Token buckets separate burst allowance from refill per minute and key budgets by account, handle, address or webhook as appropriate.
Correct password attempts clear the handle guessing budget; loose address budgets accommodate many people behind office NAT.
Refused operations report time until retry without spending another token. Periodic sweeping removes refilled buckets so memory follows active callers.
Per-account/per-app in-flight callback caps limit slow endpoints; separate ceilings limit response URLs, triggers and open forms.
Buckets are intentionally in memory: restart permits one fresh burst in exchange for avoiding a database write on every admission.

entries.plain: Starts the server on its own and runs the host's backup, restore and account recovery commands.
entries.summary: Runs the standalone server and its operator commands.
details: Parses flags/environment, validates startup values, locates the built web client and chooses LAN or isolated loopback hosting.
Dispatches backup, verify-backup, restore and local account recovery commands before ordinary server startup.
Verification prints the consequences of starting a backup: app callbacks, queued messages, accepted sessions and host settings that must be configured again.
Ordinary startup reports reachable addresses and first-owner claim information, advertises discovery when enabled and handles process shutdown.
This is an executable entry point; desktop embedding uses the library API instead.

--name, --invite-only and --access-policy set up a new workspace only. On a workspace that already has an owner the stored name and rule win, and the start prints one line for each flag that disagrees (keptSettingsNotes).

entries.plain: Announces the workspace on the local network so the app can find it without anyone typing an address.
entries.summary: Publishes a workspace discovery announcement on the local network.
details: Bonjour advertises the shared service type, port, workspace name, server/protocol versions and per-start instance ID.
The instance ID can be compared with /api/health to distinguish the intended local server from another listener on the same port.
The returned stop handle removes the service and destroys Bonjour resources during server shutdown.
Discovery helps locate a server; it does not authenticate a person or grant channel access.

entries.plain: Works out where each connection really comes from, without believing addresses that a visitor could fake.
entries.summary: Separates trusted connection identity from caller-controlled forwarding headers.
details: originFromConnection builds an origin from the socket's local address/port, correctly bracketing IPv6 rather than trusting Host.
A loopback browser origin must match host and port for first-owner local admission; a different service on the same computer is not the same origin.
Rate-limit identity normally uses the socket peer. An explicitly trusted loopback proxy may supply a valid Cloudflare address or the rightmost forwarded hop.
Ambiguous or invalid forwarded values are rejected, and non-loopback peers cannot gain proxy trust by writing those headers.

entries.plain: Sends requests to outside apps with time and size limits and, by default, keeps them off the host's private network.
entries.summary: Makes bounded integration POST requests while protecting the host's private network.
details: Private IPv4/IPv6 ranges and literal private hosts are blocked by default. DNS checks run inside the actual socket lookup, closing the check/connect gap used by DNS rebinding.
Redirects are not followed because a public endpoint could redirect to a private target. The host may deliberately allow private hooks for LAN bots.
Responses have a byte ceiling plus inactivity and whole-request deadlines, preventing an endpoint from holding a connection indefinitely with a slow stream.
Shutdown AbortSignal cancels calls and releases listeners; typed errors distinguish blocked, unreachable, timeout, too-large and aborted failures.

entries.plain: Makes sure only one server at a time can open and change a workspace folder.
entries.summary: Ensures one process owns a writable workspace folder at a time.
details: A small SQLite lock database holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE for the owner's lifetime before the workspace database and blob accounting are opened.
OS file locking releases the hold after a crash; no stale PID heuristic is needed. Alternate spellings or filesystem aliases reach the same underlying lock.
A separate owner description supplies useful process/host/purpose/port information when a second writer is refused; the description is not the locking authority.
release is safe to repeat. The guarantee depends on filesystem lock behavior, so a network share that does not honor SQLite locking cannot provide it.

holdWorkspacePath locks a sibling <folder>.lock, so the path stays held while restore renames folders; holdWorkspace takes it before making or locking the folder. The file is removed on release, and acquisition compares the file's identity before and after locking so a file its last holder removed is not taken for the lock.

entries.plain: Lets the host get someone back into their account with a temporary password, from the computer that holds the workspace.
entries.summary: Restores access to a human account from the machine that owns the workspace files.
details: Recovery refuses a workspace already held by a server and opens the database directly under an exclusive hold; no unauthenticated remote recovery endpoint exists.
It issues a temporary password, revokes all existing sessions, reactivates the account if needed and forces a new password before ordinary workspace use.
Optional makeOwner demotes any prior owner to admin and promotes the recovered human account, preserving a path back when an owner has left.
The changes and host-origin audit entry are transactional; handles close and the hold releases on every exit. Bot accounts are refused because they use tokens.

entries.plain: Hides invite codes, sign-in keys and other secrets from the server's logs, keeping the rest of each line useful.
entries.summary: Keeps request logs useful without copying URL and header credentials.
details: Sensitive path segments cover invitation codes, incoming webhook tokens and command response capabilities. Sensitive query values include download, token, ticket, code and secret.
Authorization, cookies and signature headers are removed by logger configuration; request URLs are serialized through redactUrl.
N01 catches malformed percent encoding in a query name and masks both name and value instead of throwing before the route error boundary.
The real child-server regression verifies subsequent requests still succeed. New secret-bearing routes must be added to this explicit inventory.

entries.plain: Checks the host's settings for the servers that help huddle calls connect across networks.
entries.summary: Validates host-supplied STUN/TURN configuration for browser peer connections.
details: The schema allows bounded STUN, STUNS, TURN and TURNS URLs with optional username/credential, capped numbers of configurations and URLs.
Environment JSON is parsed once with an actionable configuration error when malformed.
The server exposes authorized configuration; peer media uses WebRTC directly or the configured relay rather than flowing through Gateway.

entries.plain: Sets up a relay, from Cloudflare or elsewhere, that carries huddle audio and video when two networks will not connect directly.
entries.summary: A TURN relay for calls between networks that will not connect directly: Cloudflare's, or any other.
details: callRelaySchema accepts a Cloudflare TURN key (ID and API token) or another relay's turn:/turns: addresses, username and password. relayFromEnvironment reads a Cloudflare key from TANDEM_CLOUDFLARE_TURN_KEY_ID and TANDEM_CLOUDFLARE_TURN_API_TOKEN, both or neither.

cloudflareIceServers asks Cloudflare's credential endpoint for a password that lasts a day, leaves out port 53 (browsers block it), and turns refusals into words a host can act on without repeating the token.

createRelaySource reuses one Cloudflare password for an hour and one request for everyone joining at once; after a refusal calls go without a relay for 30 seconds before it asks again, and error() says why. withRelay adds the relay after the workspace's own servers, leaving out an address already given.

entries.plain: Sets the safety rules a browser follows on Tandem's pages, such as running only Tandem's own code.
entries.summary: Defines browser and desktop content policies that fit a multi-workspace chat client.
details: Scripts are restricted to self; object embedding and framing are denied. Blob/data image and worker sources support previews and compiled assets.
Connections intentionally allow different workspace addresses because one static client may join servers other than the page host.
The desktop meta policy omits frame-ancestors because browsers cannot enforce that directive through a meta element.
No-referrer reduces URL-token leakage on external navigation; nosniff and X-Frame-Options supplement the CSP.

entries.plain: The heart of the server, which answers the app, checks who may do what, saves messages and files, and runs background chores.
entries.summary: Composes the workspace HTTP API, authorization, background work and lifecycle.
details: Creates the exclusive workspace owner, upgraded Store, Fastify routes, Gateway, attachment budget and timers. Shared validation and permission checks enforce auth, membership, roles and password-change restrictions.

Message creation atomically validates target/thread/files, checks account-scoped nonce identity, writes the message, send key and event, and completes a schedule when applicable. Fan-out happens after commit.

Event subscribers are queued inside the event transaction; per-event actor, bot membership and body work is reused across subscribers. Delivery and file-removal pumps have limits, retries and operational failure reporting.

Every change to an account's scheduled queue (queued, edited, moved, cancelled, sent, failed, or held for a new reason) sends that account's own sockets a private scheduled event, announced by scheduledEvents in the ready snapshot, so an open Scheduled list reads the queue again at once (UX-08).

Retention removes whole eligible threads in bounded passes and publishes history.removed after commit. Upload streams reserve chunks before writing so simultaneous uploads cannot exceed the storage budget.
N08 permits one callback in flight per modal ID, returns 409 view_submitting to overlap, and releases exclusion for correction/retry. A foreign account cannot consume the owner's form.
N09 checks a pressed message's text/edit/actions fingerprint before delayed replace/delete. A missing or externally changed origin is a no-op; the same response URL can advance its own result.
Shutdown stops new work, aborts outbound requests and closes sockets/listeners/database/ownership in coordinated retryable cleanup. The library also exposes operations used by desktop hosting.

The file is an orchestration boundary with many domains; narrower modules carry SQL, crypto, networking and parsing. Callback exclusion cannot promise exactly-once business effects after an uncertain external retry.

Who may join is an access policy (invite_only, account_required, guest_allowed) kept with the legacy invite_only flag in one write. POST /api/auth/guest admits a display name alone while guests are allowed and an owner exists, rationed by address and capped at 200 live guests; POST /api/auth/guest/account converts the same identity to a member and replaces its sessions. requireUser refuses a guest any route outside GUEST_ROUTES, so new routes start closed to guests; guests cannot be put in private rooms, DMs or friendships, sign in with a password, or be promoted or reset by an admin. Turning guests off revokes their sessions and sockets.

A status can end by itself (UX-61): PATCH /api/me takes statusExpiresAt, and a new status without one drops an earlier end. One timer waits for the soonest end, clears every status due then and sends user.updated to everyone, as if its owner had cleared it; on start it clears what ended while the server was stopped.

A slash command whose app answered an error status, could not be reached or was blocked answers ok: false, command_failed, with the reason in message as well as in the private note to the channel, for the test in Apps and integrations (UX-63). Older clients read only ok and error.

The workspace's name and who may join belong to the workspace (UX-60). PUT /api/admin/workspace/name and /access-policy, owner or admin only, go through renameWorkspace and changeAccessPolicy, the same functions the desktop host's setWorkspaceName, setAccessPolicy and setInviteOnly call, so the two cannot drift. Each writes the audit record in the same transaction (the host as a null actor), tells every socket (workspace.renamed, workspace.accessPolicy), signs guests out with their sockets when they are no longer allowed, and tells onWorkspaceChange listeners. The start options workspaceName, accessPolicy and inviteOnly set up a workspace with no accounts only; once it has one, a start never puts back an older choice.

entries.plain: Checks every live message the app sends, such as typing or huddle signals, before the server acts on it.
entries.summary: Checks socket payloads at the server boundary before Gateway trusts them.
details: A discriminated union admits hello, ping, typing, huddle join/leave and signaling with bounded IDs, tokens and cursors.
Offer/answer SDP, ICE candidates and media state have explicit size and numeric constraints, keeping untrusted JSON within supported shapes.
Protocol TypeScript types alone cannot validate a remote caller; this Zod schema provides runtime enforcement without importing browser DOM types.
Validates huddle.report: counts, states and enums only, so a report cannot carry an address or arbitrary text.

entries.plain: Keeps track of how much space uploaded files use and stops uploads before they go over the host's limit.
entries.summary: Accounts for stored blobs and reserves upload bytes before concurrent writes.
details: Startup inventories regular blob files; reserve adds each accepted chunk to that file's accounting only if the total remains within the configured ceiling.
release removes all counted bytes for a blob after failed upload or successful cleanup, and storedIds enables database/blob reconciliation.
Chunk reservation permits many small uploads without pessimistically reserving the maximum file size for each.
Two uploads can each reserve part of the remaining space and both need retry; recoverable refusal is the tradeoff for never overspending the limit.

entries.plain: Reads and writes everything in the workspace's database, from accounts and channels to messages, search and who can see what.
entries.summary: Maps workspace rules to transactional SQLite records and authorized query results.
details: Owns account/session/channel/membership CRUD, per-user read/follow/save state, messages/files, invitations, audit records, integrations and durable queues. Visibility checks remain part of history and search queries.

Message hydration batches reactions, reply counts, pins and file metadata for a page instead of running one query per message. Indexed mentions support unread counts without reparsing the entire history.

Search combines safe quoted FTS terms, filename matches and structured filters. Rare terms start from matches; common terms try a newest-message window first and fill from older matches, preserving ordering and visibility.

N06 soft deletion blanks words and actions, clears associated reaction/pin/save/mention state and redacts older event copies, including file names/buttons. Event sequence records remain so reconnect order still works.
N07 markScheduledSent keeps status and message linkage while clearing text/file IDs and releasing scheduled-file holds in the message transaction.
Whole-thread purge uses a temporary ID table, retains only minimal send-key tombstones to prevent retry resurrection, queues blob deletions and redacts event/delivery copies together.

Due cleanup and app delivery queries isolate retrying/rejected rows so a failing item does not block healthy work. Follow-state revisions prevent stale authoritative echoes from replacing newer state.
Already delivered app copies and prior backups are outside active-store cleanup; the SQL rules do not constitute physical disk erasure.

Inline replies keep the message they answer (reply_to_id) and whether its author was notified (reply_ping). Hydration reads each quoted message as it now is, cut to replyExcerpt, or says it was deleted; a notified author is indexed as mentioned. Editing, deleting or purging a quoted message rewrites the quotes in its replies' logged copies too, so the log never keeps words that were taken back.

Guest sessions keep their 24-hour expiry instead of sliding; canAccess and listChannelsVisibleTo give a guest public channels only, whatever membership it might hold. convertGuest turns a guest into a member in place, and revokeGuestSessions reports the ended tokens so their sockets close.
listPins also counts every pin it would list (deleted messages and replies in deleted threads left out), so the header's pinned line can say how many from one row (UX-23).

A member's own choices for a conversation (notify level, muted, starred) live on their membership row, read in one shape by toPrefs for the ready snapshot, channel.access and the prefs route. Another member's row, and so their choices, is never touched.

entries.plain: Names the server's version and the exact code it was built from, for backups and network announcements.
entries.summary: Names the server version and exposes source identity stamped into builds.
details: A small standalone module avoids loading HTTP, sockets and discovery just to label a backup or announcement.
Built output includes revision and dirty state; source execution reports no build stamp rather than inventing one.
Version describes the release interface while revision/dirty identifies the actual source behind an artifact.

entries.plain: Tells browsers how long to keep saved copies of the web version's files, so pages load fast and updates arrive cleanly.
entries.summary: Applies cache rules that keep static delivery fast and upgrades coherent.
details: Content-hashed assets receive a one-year immutable cache lifetime because changing content produces a different filename.
HTML and other stable names use no-cache so a browser revalidates the page that points to the current asset hashes.
A missing /assets/ request returns a genuine asset miss rather than the single-page application's HTML; an obsolete JavaScript chunk should not be delivered as HTML.

entries.plain: The shared rules for finding a workspace on the local network and for building invite links that open in Tandem.
entries.summary: Shares LAN discovery and invitation-link addressing conventions.
details: Defines the mDNS service type, default port and TXT fields including the per-start instance ID used by health verification.
hostWithPort brackets IPv6 literals correctly; isLinkableAddress excludes zone-specific and link-local addresses that ordinary browser URLs cannot use.
Tandem is the primary deep-link scheme; Gatherline and SlackOSS schemes remain accepted so old invitations keep opening.

entries.plain: The shared rules for what a person, channel, message, file and every other workspace record looks like.
entries.summary: Defines the shared vocabulary of workspace records and feature metadata.
details: Models users/roles, room types, memberships, messages, files, actions, invitations, audits, sessions, schedules, apps and forms without coupling the server to React or browser DOM objects.

Message seq identifies its creation event; a live payload can have seq 0 until the client applies the envelope's sequence. Thread replies and channel-broadcast replies remain the same underlying message.
Follow records include revision and unread-hold state; operational status models storage, queues, retention, connections and event-loop delay.
Optional capability/metadata fields allow older servers and clients to interoperate without assuming support.
The shared 30-day send retry window aligns client automatic retries with server retention of minimal send keys after content is removed.
Role includes guest, and ServerInfo.accessPolicy says who may join; an older server omits it, which clients read as accounts only.
ChannelPrefs.starred is one account's star on a conversation (UX-20). Servers before schema 40 leave it out, which reads as unstarred.
AuditAction includes workspace.renamed and workspace.access_policy_changed, with the target type workspace, recorded with the old and new value.

entries.plain: Describes the updates the server sends, both the ones replayed after a reconnect and short-lived ones like typing.
entries.summary: Defines durable replay events and private/live socket messages.
details: WorkspaceEvent covers durable message, channel, membership and user changes; EventEnvelope adds monotonically increasing seq for reconnect replay.
history.removed names whole thread roots so clients can invalidate removed root/reply content and files even when history is evicted.

EphemeralEvent carries presence, typing, read/unread changes, private saves/preferences/follows, correlated huddle admission and one-user app replies/forms; these are never replayed as durable history.
ReadySnapshot describes current visible state and replayFrom, while synced marks completion. A null replay cursor replaces cached history; resync is the legacy fallback.
The distinction lets a lost ephemeral notice recover through a new snapshot without preserving private/transient UI messages forever.
Flags on ReadySnapshot (huddleReports, inlineReplies, scheduledEvents, activityThreads, stars) say what this server does, so a client offers nothing an older server would refuse or quietly drop.
workspace.accessPolicy tells everyone signed in who may join now, and ReadySnapshot.workspaceSettings says the server takes Workspace settings' changes (UX-60). Older clients ignore the event.

entries.plain: Shared formatting rules for showing text exactly as typed and spotting @channel, @here and @everyone mentions.
entries.summary: Shares literal mrkdwn escaping and room-wide mention interpretation.
details: escapeMrkdwn prefixes formatting delimiters and backslashes so generated text such as /shrug is displayed literally.
broadcastsIn recognizes Slack-compatible <!channel>, <!here> and <!everyone> tokens, normalizing everyone to channel.
broadcastLabel turns wire tokens into user-facing labels; choosing who is eligible for notification remains an authorization/presence decision elsewhere.

entries.plain: The shared rules for the messages that set up a huddle, including which side starts the call so both do not at once.
entries.summary: Describes peer-call signaling and deterministic offer ownership.
details: Offer, answer, ICE and explicit camera/screen/muted messages are plain serializable objects usable by both server and browser.
Explicit media flags distinguish an active camera from a silent negotiated slot; a receiver track's muted flag alone is not evidence that frames exist.
shouldInitiateOffer uses user-ID ordering so two peers discovering each other do not both offer simultaneously.
HuddleState lists live participants. The protocol carries handshake/control state rather than audio or video bytes.
CallReport, CallCause, CandidateKind and CallLogEntry describe what a side saw of a connection and the server's call log, without addresses or SDP.

entries.plain: Gathers all the shared rules in one place so the app and the server use exactly the same ones.
entries.summary: Exports the common protocol modules through one package entry.
details: Re-exports entity, event, REST validation, discovery, search, formatting, huddle and permission contracts.
Server, client and UI consume the same names instead of copying request shapes or subtly different policies.
Runtime helper/schema imports can affect bundling, so constants needed by lightweight consumers are kept outside schema-heavy definitions where practical.

entries.plain: Decides who can manage a channel, such as adding or removing people, with the same rules in the app and on the server.
entries.summary: Shares channel-management policy between server enforcement and UI affordances.
details: Owner/admin, creator and delegated member managers receive different management powers; active human status and room type are checked.
Delegated management ends with membership. Removing someone is not a public-room ban, and an administrator's management role does not grant visibility into private rooms.
Removal protects self, owner, admins and privileged managers according to the actor's authority; manager assignment rejects inappropriate bot/deactivated/creator targets.
Visibility must be checked separately by the server even when a management helper returns true.

entries.plain: Checks the shape and size of everything the app sends the server, such as names, passwords, messages and scheduled sends.
entries.summary: Validates the shared HTTP request bodies and paging/search parameters.
details: Zod schemas bound handles, passwords, profile fields, channel types, message text/files, scheduling, integration URLs, form values, administrative updates and cursor formats.
Messages require words or attachments; DM creation has a fixed counterpart count and group DMs have a bounded participant list.
Scheduling carries a stable nonce; editing a scheduled message carries expectedText so a conflicting edit can be refused.
Integration URLs reject embedded credentials and non-HTTP(S) schemes. Modal submissions bound nested IDs and values before echoing them to an app.
Types are inferred from the schemas, keeping compile-time client contracts aligned with the server's runtime parsing. Parsed shape alone does not imply authorization.
channelPrefsBody takes notifyLevel, muted and starred, each optional. An older server's schema drops starred without an error, which is why clients wait for ReadySnapshot.stars.

workspaceNameSchema is the one rule for a workspace's name, for its host and its admins: 1 to 80 characters once trimmed, no control characters. workspaceNameBody and accessPolicyBody are Workspace settings' requests (UX-60).

entries.plain: Understands search filters such as who sent it, where, and on which day, the same way in the app and on the server.
entries.summary: Parses search syntax and calendar-day filters identically on client and server.
details: Splits recognized from/in/has/type/before/after modifiers from free terms, records invalid calendar dates and normalizes handles/channel names.
Attachment categories map to MIME patterns and filename extensions for server SQL, letting UI hints describe the same filters the server applies.
before excludes the named day; after starts at the following day in the reader's IANA timezone. Day boundaries account for daylight-saving transitions instead of assuming 24 hours.
A bounded cache keeps at most 32 Intl.DateTimeFormat instances, avoiding repeated construction while preventing arbitrary timezone inputs from growing memory indefinitely.
This parser returns criteria; Store still adds current conversation visibility and safe query parameter handling.

flows.title: Signing in and catching up
flows.summary: Signing in with a password gives the app a sign-in key. The live connection then turns that key into an up-to-date view of the workspace, filling in missed updates only where it is safe.

steps.title: Check the request and limit guessing
steps.description: The server checks the sign-in form has the right shape. It limits wrong passwords per username and per network address, to slow down guessing. It believes what a middleman says about who is connecting only when the host turned that on and the middleman runs on the same computer.
steps.detail: REST schemas check the login body. Separate address and handle allowances bound guessing; proxy headers only count under explicit loopback trust.

steps.title: Check the password and start a session
steps.description: The server compares the password against a scrambled copy, never the password itself. If it matches, the server sends back a random sign-in key. It keeps only a scrambled copy of that key, with an expiry date and the account it belongs to.
steps.detail: scrypt verification checks the stored salt/hash. Only a random bearer token leaves the server; the session row stores its hash, expiry and account identity.

steps.title: Say hello before getting updates
steps.description: The app opens a live connection and says which version it speaks and the last update it saw. The server checks the sign-in is still valid and whether the account must change its password first. Only then does it load the whole workspace for this person and start sending live updates.
steps.detail: The socket schema validates protocol/version/cursor. Gateway checks the session and forced password-change state and reads the full snapshot before registering the connection.

steps.title: Fill in missed updates or start fresh
steps.description: If the app was away briefly, the server sends the updates it missed, leaving out channels the person can no longer see. If the app was away too long, or its place in the history is gone, the server tells it to replace its copy of the workspace. Either way, a final signal tells the app it is up to date.
steps.detail: Store filters replay to current public/member access. If the cursor is pruned, invalid or beyond the replay budget, ready requests replacement; otherwise missed events replay and synced finishes catch-up.

steps.title: Keep checking the sign-in
steps.description: The server checks the sign-in again as it sends updates and during regular check-ins. When a sign-in ends, the server cuts its connections. Who is online comes from who is connected right now, and is worked out again after a reconnect.
steps.detail: Delivery and heartbeats recheck sessions; revocation disconnects affected sockets. Ephemeral presence is derived from live socket groups and rebuilt at reconnect.

flows.detail: Authentication produces a session; the socket handshake turns it into visible current state plus any safe replay.

flows.title: Saving a message on the server
flows.summary: The server saves a message the same way whether someone sends it now or it was scheduled earlier. Saving and announcing happen in a fixed order, so what is saved and what everyone sees always agree.

steps.title: Check the message and its files
steps.description: The server checks the message is within size limits, the sender's account is active and they can post in this channel. The channel must not be archived, and a reply must point at a real thread. Attached files must belong to this person and channel, and not already be set aside for another scheduled message.
steps.detail: Parse bounded message input, check active account/current channel access, archived state and a valid root. Files must belong to this account/channel and cannot be promised to another schedule.

steps.title: Spot a repeated send
steps.description: Each send carries a one-time code chosen by the sender's device. If the same code comes again with the same content, the server returns the message it already saved instead of posting a second copy. If the content differs, or that message was since deleted or cleared away by old-history cleanup, the server refuses.
steps.detail: Hash the request shape under the account-scoped nonce. An identical retry returns its message; conflicting content or a key for deleted/retained history is refused rather than creating a second post.

steps.title: Save the message and its update together
steps.description: In one step, the server saves the message, links its files, records its code and writes the update that announces it. The same step records deliveries to outside apps that should hear about it. Either all of this is saved or none of it is.
steps.detail: Create and hydrate the message, attach files, record its request key and append message.created in one synchronous transaction. Eligible app delivery rows are queued with that event.

steps.title: Mark a scheduled message as sent
steps.description: For a scheduled message, the same step marks the schedule as sent, links it to the new message and clears the schedule's own copy of the words and file list. A crash cannot leave one half done without the other.
steps.detail: For a scheduled send, the same transaction marks the schedule sent, links the message and clears queue text/file IDs. A crash cannot commit only one side.

steps.title: Announce it after saving
steps.description: Only once everything is saved does the server send the update to people allowed to see it. It groups together the updates for people following the thread or mentioned in it. Deliveries to outside apps go out separately, with a limited number of retries.
steps.detail: Gateway fans out only committed events under current visibility. Targeted follow/mention updates are coalesced, while app deliveries run through the bounded retry pump.

flows.detail: The same posting path handles direct sends and due schedules so persistence and live publication agree.

flows.title: Pressing a button on an app's message
flows.summary: Short-lived permissions tie each button press and form to the right app and person, and to what they may see right now. Extra checks handle a form sent twice at once and replies that arrive late.

steps.title: Show only buttons Tandem supports
steps.description: Apps lay out their messages the way Slack apps do. The server keeps only text, buttons that open a web link and buttons that tell the app they were pressed, all within size limits. The message a button sits on decides which app and conversation the press belongs to.
steps.detail: Block Kit text/actions become bounded native text and HTTP(S) link or callback buttons. The pressed message determines the owning bot and conversation.

steps.title: Give the app short-lived permission
steps.description: When someone presses a button, the server tells the app and hands it two short-lived permissions, one to open a form and a reply address to update the message. These expire, and only so many can exist at once. Every call to an app is signed, has a time limit and cannot reach private computers on the host's network.
steps.detail: The callback receives an app-bound trigger and a response URL. Capability maps cap memory and expire permissions; outbound calls are signed, deadline-bounded and private-host-checked.

steps.title: Open the form for the right person
steps.description: The app uses its permission once to open a form. The server first checks that the app, its bot, the person and the channel are all still allowed. It then sends the form, with only the kinds of fields Tandem supports, to that person alone.
steps.detail: views.open consumes one matching trigger after current app, bot, person and channel checks. Supported fields become a view.open ephemeral event for the owner alone.

steps.title: Refuse a second submission at the same time
steps.description: When the person submits, the server checks the form is theirs, required answers are filled in and each choice comes from the list. Only one submission of a form can be on its way to the app at a time, and a second one meanwhile is refused. Once the first finishes, the person can correct their answers or try again.
steps.detail: The server verifies form ownership, required values and select options. One modal ID may have one callback in flight; overlap receives 409 view_submitting, and finally releases exclusion for correction or deliberate retry.

steps.title: Ignore late changes to an old message
steps.description: The app may later ask to replace or delete the message whose button was pressed. The server does this only if the message still looks as it did when pressed, and ignores the request if it was changed or deleted since. Each successful update through the same reply address becomes the version the next one must match.
steps.detail: Before replace/delete, current text/edit/actions must match the pressed revision. A disappeared or changed origin is ignored; successful updates through the same response URL advance its own expected revision.

steps.title: Know what a retry can still repeat
steps.description: The server stops overlapping submissions and checks again that permission was not withdrawn. Still, an app may act on a submission and then lose the connection before answering. If the person tries again, the app should spot the repeat by the form's ID.
steps.detail: The server prevents overlap and rechecks revocation, but an endpoint may perform its business effect before a transport failure. An app should deduplicate a retried view_submission by view ID.

flows.detail: Short-lived capabilities tie actions to the right app/person and current access, while N08/N09 control overlapping and delayed replies.

flows.title: Deleting messages and clearing old history
flows.summary: Deleting a message or clearing old history removes its words, buttons and file links from every working copy the server keeps, not just the one you see. The order of past updates stays intact, and a delayed resend cannot bring a deleted message back.

steps.title: Choose what to remove
steps.description: Deleting a message clears its words and buttons and anything live tied to it. If the host set history to expire, cleanup picks a thread only once its newest reply is old enough, then removes the whole thread. Each cleanup round handles a limited amount.
steps.detail: Soft deletion clears one message's words/actions and associated live state. Retention chooses roots only when their newest reply is old enough and removes the whole thread within a bounded pass.

steps.title: Clean up everything in one step
steps.description: The server handles even a very large thread in one go. It removes message and file links, keeps a bare record of each send code, lines up files for deletion and blanks stored copies of updates and app deliveries. It saves all of this together.
steps.detail: A temporary ID table handles large threads without bind-count limits. Message/file references, minimal purged send keys, queued blob deletions and redacted event/delivery copies commit together.

steps.title: Keep the order without the old words
steps.description: The server keeps a numbered list of past updates so apps can catch up in order. Updates that are out of date because the message was deleted or changed stay in that list, but lose their words, file details and button labels and links. A database upgrade also cleans copies left by earlier versions, including scheduled messages already sent.
steps.detail: Superseded event rows stay in the ordered replay log but lose text, file metadata and button labels/values/URLs. Schema 37 repairs earlier deleted/superseded copies and sent schedules.

steps.title: Tell connected people what was removed
steps.description: Once saved, the server tells everyone allowed to see it that a message was deleted or that history was cleared. For a whole thread it names the thread, so each person's app drops its saved copies of the thread and its replies and stops any file transfers for them.
steps.detail: After commit, message.deleted or history.removed reaches authorized sockets. Whole-thread root IDs let clients invalidate evicted root/reply caches and pending attachment transfers.

steps.title: Delete the files, retrying when needed
steps.description: A background job deletes the files a few at a time, and counts storage space as freed only once a file is gone. It tries a failed file again after a wait and keeps the failure visible, while the other files go ahead.
steps.detail: The file pump deletes bounded pages and releases storage accounting only after success. Retry delay and rejected rows let healthy removals proceed while failures remain visible.

steps.title: Know what cleanup does not reach
steps.description: These steps clean the copies in the working database. They do not remove the content from older backups, securely wipe space the database freed on disk, or recall what was already sent to outside apps.
steps.detail: Active database copies are cleaned. Historical backups, freed storage blocks and payloads already delivered to external apps are not recalled or securely erased by these operations.

flows.detail: N06/N07 and earlier retention work remove redundant words, actions and file references while preserving replay order and retry safety.

flows.title: Backing up and restoring a workspace
flows.summary: A backup is built and checked in full before it counts as a backup. Restoring keeps the original workspace, but a known gap remains while the folders swap.

steps.title: Copy the database at one moment
steps.description: The server copies its database as it stands, including the most recent saves, and lists the uploaded files the backup needs. If a file is deleted while the backup runs, the backup fails. To be sure a backup is complete, take it while the server is stopped.
steps.detail: VACUUM INTO reads committed SQLite/WAL state; snapshot file inventory identifies required blobs. Missing concurrent-deleted blobs fail capture, so stopped-server capture is the way to guarantee completeness.

steps.title: Check the backup before keeping it
steps.description: The copied database and files must match their recorded sizes and fingerprints, the expected layout and counts, and the database's own health check. Every file reference must be valid, with nothing listed twice and nothing pointing outside the backup. Only then does the server move the finished backup to its final place.
steps.detail: Staged database and files must match checksums/sizes, schema/counts, integrity and references, with no manifest duplicates or path escape. Only then is the complete capture renamed to its destination.

steps.title: See what a restored copy would do
steps.description: Without changing anything, the host can list which outside apps a restored copy would contact, which scheduled messages are waiting, which app calls never went out and which sign-ins still work. A separate isolated mode runs the copy without calling apps or sending scheduled messages, so it can be looked at safely.
steps.detail: Read-only inventory reports app destinations, queued schedules, undelivered callbacks and surviving sessions. Isolated mode blocks app calls and schedule delivery while inspecting a restored copy.

steps.title: Prepare the restore beside the original
steps.description: Restore refuses to start if a server is using the workspace. It copies the checked backup next to the workspace folder and checks the copy again. The old workspace moves to a set-aside folder so it can still be recovered.
steps.detail: Restore refuses an already held workspace, copies the verified backup beside the target and verifies staged bytes. The old workspace is moved to a superseded folder for recovery.

steps.title: No other server can slip in while folders swap
steps.description: Restore has to let go of the workspace folder for a moment to rename it, because Windows will not rename a folder with a file open inside it. It keeps a second claim beside the folder the whole time, so a server started in that moment is refused and makes no workspace of its own there. If the swap fails, the original goes back where it was.
steps.detail: Restore holds a sibling path lock from before staging until publication or rollback is complete, and releases the in-folder hold only for the renames. holdWorkspace takes the path lock before mkdir, so a concurrent start gets WorkspaceInUseError and the target stays absent until the staged copy is renamed in.

steps.title: Start the restored workspace as usual
steps.description: The next server to start takes sole hold of the restored workspace and upgrades its database if needed, keeping a copy from before the upgrade. The host applies settings that belong to the computer separately, such as the public address, how long history is kept and call connection settings.
steps.detail: A subsequent server opens with the exclusive writer hold and atomic migrations, taking pre-upgrade copies when needed. Local host settings such as public URL, retention and ICE configuration must be applied separately.

flows.detail: Backups are staged and validated before publication; restore preserves the original and holds the target's path through folder replacement.
